A riveted iron lattice tower standing hard left of centre, carrying three pairs of long timber semaphore blades one above the other: the top pair both raised to forty-five degrees, the middle pair flat out level, the lowest pair hanging straight down. Every blade is painted signal-red with a broad white band across its middle and a white ring at its tip.

A tall iron frame holding a bank of six square timber shutters, four of them tilted right over edge-on so the sky shows straight through the gaps and two swung shut flat to the frame. Each shutter is painted deep bottle-green with one bold white chevron on it, and a nest of cranks and rods runs down the frame's leg.

One spindle carrying three cast-iron discs the size of cartwheels — the outer two turned face-on to us, the middle one turned edge-on so it reads as a thin dark bar. Their faces are painted matte black with a single fat white circle at the centre, and a counterweight hangs on a chain below them.

A slender iron standard carrying two lamps in big brass hoods, one above the other: the upper lamp burning a hot orange, the lower one dark and cold. The hoods are painted white inside so the lit one throws a soft coloured disc onto the timber behind it, and the spare lamp hangs on a hook at the standard's foot.

A slim iron tower crowned with a tiny timber cabin no bigger than a garden shed, its four small windows blazing from within and a stovepipe on its roof trailing a thread of smoke. An open ironwork gallery runs round it, and one pair of blades above it is dropped to the straight-down safe position.

A great cable drum on a squat iron carriage, wound tight with new bright wire, a long crank handle standing out from its side and a pawl dropped into its ratchet teeth. Its cheeks are painted oxide red, and a second empty drum lies on its side beside it with the last few turns of old wire still on it.

Three towers strung across the roofs at three different heights — the near one a riveted lattice filling the left third of the frame, the second half as tall away to the right, the third only a thin dark silhouette standing out of the far band of city. Each carries one pair of blades, and no two pairs are at the same angle.

An old stone chimney adapted as a signal tower: iron brackets bolted right into its brick, a timber gallery clamped round it at the top, and one very long blade projecting straight out over the street below, raised steeply. The blade is painted white with two black bands, and a ladder of iron staples climbs the brick.

A tower head spreading a fan of eight cables that run out past the right edge of the frame, each cable ending at a turnbuckle and a heavy iron anchor ring bolted into the parapet brick. The tower's own timber facings are painted a flat cream, and a spare turnbuckle hangs off a hook in the lattice.

A pair of blades caught halfway through their swing, one rising and one falling, their timber still soft with motion blur and the chain-and-counterweight below still swinging past the vertical. The blades are painted cream with a black tip, and the crank handle is standing abandoned at the top of its stroke.

A glazed lantern room at a tower's top, its panes coloured in a row — one ruby, one clear, one deep green — with a bright lamp behind them, so a wedge of ruby light lies across the leads and a wedge of green lies beside it. The lantern's ironwork is painted white and the roof above it is a little copper cone.

A tower built of two old iron rails bolted back to back, guyed with four wires to ring-bolts in the roof, carrying a single broad paddle on a spindle at head height, the paddle swung right over to horizontal. The paddle is painted quartered black and white, and a grease pot hangs from the spindle bracket.

A massive timber A-frame tower, tarred black, carrying a crossbar with four short vanes on it like the stubs of a windmill — two vanes up, two vanes down. Each vane is painted a different solid colour, and a rope ladder hangs down the frame's inside face.

A signal staff rising off the parapet with a solid flag hauled right to its truck and standing out stiff in the wind — a red rectangle with a white square at its middle — the halyard cracking against the staff and a second flag bundled at the staff's foot ready to go up.

A tower's whole upper works are a nest of pulleys and taut wires, eight sheaves in iron cheeks all pulling different ways, with one long blade at the top of it all standing straight up. The pulley cheeks are painted oxide red, and a man's mallet is wedged between two of the wires.

A short, fat, round brick tower with an iron collar at its top carrying two paddles on a horizontal axle, one paddle swung to point at the sky and the other to point at the ground. They are painted white with a black centre spot, and a bell in a little iron hood hangs under the collar.

A tower whose blades are worked from the roof by a long vertical rod and a foot treadle on a plank platform, the rod running up through three guide brackets. The treadle's tread is worn shiny, both blades are raised steeply, and a hobnail-scarred plank is nailed across for footing.

Two towers standing close together with a plank bridge slung between their galleries on ropes, the bridge sagging in the middle, both towers carrying a single blade and both blades pointing the same way — flat out level. The galleries are painted cream and the tower legs are tarred black.

A tower head carrying a horizontal drum with eight small paddles set round it like a paddle-wheel, four of them showing their painted white faces and four turned edge-on. A crank and a worm gear turn the drum, and the whole assembly is hooded above by a little lead roof.

A tall lattice tower with its top third clearly newer than the rest — bright galvanised iron bolted onto old black-painted iron, with the join wrapped in wire. It carries three blades in a row across its head, all three hanging straight down, each painted red with a white tip.

A tower standing right on the parapet corner with its four feet in cast-iron shoes bedded in lead, the roof's own stone parapet running away from it both sides. One pair of blades is raised to forty-five degrees and a small brass lamp burns green under them on its own bracket.

A signal tower built into a stone bell turret, the old bell still hanging in the arch below and a new iron cage bolted above it holding two paddles, one flat and one on edge. The paddles are painted cream with a black diagonal, and pigeon wire is stretched across the arch.

A squat iron mounting bolted straight to the tiles, no tower at all: a single tall blade on a pivot rising out of it to twice a man's height, raised steeply, with its counterweight box resting on the tiles beside it full of scrap iron. The blade is painted white with three black bands.

A tower's gallery hung about with the whole kit of the trade — coils of wire on pegs, three mallets in a rack, a hank of tarred twine, a grease pot, a boat-hook, a spare paddle leaned against the rail — and above it two blades, one up and one level. The rail is painted cream and the pegs are bare iron.

A tower carrying a wide horizontal beam with two long vanes at its ends, the whole beam tilted so one vane points high and the other low, the way a seesaw sits. The vanes are painted solid yellow with a black tip each, and a chain from the beam's centre runs down to a winch on the roof.
